content.title: Michigan to face Tennessee in Elite Eight Tipoff time broadcast information announced for clash
content.text: FlameThe Volunteers have beaten Miami-Ohio (78-56), 3-seed Virginia (76-72) and 2-seed Iowa State (76-62) in the NCAA Tournament so far. They are in the Elite Eight for the third consecutive season, but are still seeking their first-ever trip to the Final Four.CHICAGO, Ill. — The Michigan men's basketball team is 40 minutes away from the Final Four, and will try to get there Sunday afternoon against yet another SEC team.After taking down 4-seed Alabama with a 90-77 win Friday night, the tip-off time, broadcast information and opponent were revealed for the Wolverines' Elite Eight matchup. Michigan (19-1 Big Ten, 34-3 overall) will take on 6-seed Tennessee at the United Center Sunday, with the game tipping off at 2:15 p.m. ET and airing on CBS. The winner will advance to the Final Four, set to be played next Saturday in Indianapolis. The Volunteers (11-7 SEC, 25-11 overall) have beaten Miami-Ohio (78-56), 3-seed Virginia (76-72) and 2-seed Iowa State (76-62) in the NCAA Tournament so far. They are in the Elite Eight for the third consecutive season, but are still seeking their first-ever trip to the Final Four."It really hasn't hit me yet, to be honest with you," Tennessee coach Rick Barnes said after beating the Cyclones Friday night. "That's the honest truth. The group we got last two years prior to this, guys from day one they were with us. We came in with 11 new players. I felt like we had improved in a lot of different areas. If we could bring it all together -- and there's -- to be very honest with you, I thought we should have won more games in the regular season, but when you turned it over the way we did the last four or five minutes, that's why we've gotten better with that over the last couple of weeks finishing games."According to KenPom.com, Michigan is projected to win, 77-70, and has a 74-percent chance to win. Tennessee is 2-2 against common opponents with the Wolverines, having one 1-1 against Alabama, beating Rutgers and losing to Illinois prior this season. Rebounding will be a major point of emphasis for Michigan, as the Volunteers lead the nation in offensive rebounding rate, and rank second nationally with a rebounding margin of plus-12.7 per game. The Wolverines rank eighth nationally in rebounding margin, but Tennessee's 43-20 edge against Iowa State buried the Cyclones' hopes."We do have a standard on a lot of things," Barnes said. "It's not just what we do on the basketball court. You know, we're pretty much a no-nonsense program. We talk about that through the recruiting process. We tell everyone it's going to be tough. We want them to come and want to help them live their dreams, and along the way we would love to have a chance to play for a national championship."Michigan took down the Crimson Tide Friday evening, 90-77, thanks to a high-octane offense and a defense that improved as the game wore on. The Wolverines gave up 49 points in the game's opening 20 minutes, and 28 points in the second half. That improved defense allowed Michigan to pull away in the second half, and come away with a program-record 34th win on the season. "Once we settled into the game. And Alabama is tough to guard, as we all know. I do think they were surprised at our urgency to get back to their shooters," Michigan coach Dusty May said of the second half. "Because we didn't have the same type in the first half. There were two or three plays that jump out in my mind right when they happened I thought, that's going to have a lasting impact on this game. And it was Elliot's two blocked three on Wrightsell, and Roddy blocked another one. "When that happens, as shooters, you typically, when you get one or two blocks you start looking around instead of focusing on what you need to be looking at. I do think that had an affect on their shooting, especially the last eight or ten minutes."Now, the two teams will face off in Chicago, with a spot in the Final Four on the line.Story photo: Marc-Gregor Campredon, MGoBlog,comUnselfishness, Toughness, and Belief: Inside Michigan’s Road to the Final Four with U-M Assistant Mike BoyntonMichigan is back in the Final Four, and assistant coach Mike Boynton Jr. explains how unselfishness, toughness, and star leadership blazed the trail. From Yaxel Lendeborg’s dominance to Elliot Cadeau’s “dog mentality”, here’s an inside look at the ingredients in U-M's run to the Final Four.Michigan basketball's journey back to the Final Four has been defined by sacrifice, chemistry, and relentless growth… themes that resonate deeply with assistant coach Mike Boynton Jr. As the Wolverines prepare for a heavyweight showdown with Arizona, Boynton reflected on the foundation built nearly a year ago that made this historic run possible.“We just felt something all summer.” (Photo: Kamil Krzaczynski, USA TODAY Sports) Boynton says Michigan's rise from a team with promise to a powerhouse started early in the offseason. "We just felt something all summer, and it wasn't just about talent, because every team has talent," Boynton said. "Our guys were willing to lean into each other's strengths and bring out the best in one another. Yax showed how someone can dominate around the rim, others embraced Morez's power, and Elliot brought it all together as the ultimate connector. We felt that energy in the summer and fall. We knew it would take time to find our rhythm, but once we did, it was great to watch."“He knew he was the guy” (Photo: Kamil Krzaczynski, USA TODAY Sports) Boynton has often talked about Yaxel Lendeborg's growth, describing how the star forward has gone from being a selfless teammate, to stepping up as a leader and becoming more selfish when the team needed him most. "If we were going to be playing past this weekend, we were going to need Yax to be the best player," Boynton explained. "He talks about how we don't have a best player, but everybody knows he's the guy. This weekend, he played like he knew he was the guy, and our team needed him to be that because that was our separator." That shift didn't come overnight. Boynton said the staff had conversations throughout the season about pushing Lendeborg to take on that alpha role more aggressively. "We would get frustrated at times as a staff," Boynton recounted. "Like, 'we're rolling, but we could be on another level if you are a little more aggressive. His mentality was so unselfish. (He would say), 'hey, I have great teammates.' But you're the greatest of the teammates. We need you to be intentional about asserting that in games. At the end of the day, that lifts us all. You're the rising tide that lifts all the boats." "Yaxel led the charge in that regard," Boynton continued. "All the things that he didn't do in games that maybe he could have been more forceful and dominant with, he was never chasing stats. He never cared. He was just about us winning, and he wanted everybody to feel a part of it. A big part of him playing that way and having that mindset trickled down to the rest of our roster."“We don’t have an unlimited budget, we have guys who sacrificed” (Photo: Kamil Krzaczynski, USA TODAY Sports) Michigan's team features four transfers in the starting lineup, led by Lendeborg… a fact that has drawn considerable attention. Detractors, including some less successful coaches with outdated views on NIL and the transfer portal, believe Michigan simply spent the most money to win. Boynton dismissed those clueless notions, emphasizing that Michigan's defining traits are chemistry and selflessness. "People talk about these kids making money and how we have the highest payroll in the country. We actually don't," he said. "Probably everybody who plays on our team could be making significantly more money somewhere else than they do here because we don't have an unlimited budget. We have a budget, and everybody, including Yax, decided that they wanted to sacrifice a little bit individually so that we could do what we did together." This commitment to shared sacrifice has shaped Michigan's identity into a distinctly team-first mindset. "We have a bunch of guys who put their egos aside, who all come from different places," Boynton said. "Even the guys who returned here knew that it was going to be different and challenging for them… They blocked out the outside noise, their draft status, their professional standing, whatever it was, so that they could do something that will last forever."“He’s been playing like Chris Paul Jr.” (Photo: Kamil Krzaczynski, USA TODAY Sports) At the heart of that unselfishness is Elliot Cadeau, whom Boynton calls "the wizard" for his elite court vision and floor control. "He's been playing like Chris Paul Jr. the last two and a half weeks, the way he can control the floor," Boynton said. "We saw it in spurts during the season… On those days, he was the best point guard on the court. That kid's been unbelievable." Boynton said Cadeau's relentless competitiveness and emotional leadership, has become just as important as his skills. "Elliot has a presence about him," Boynton explained. "He's got a mentality that's contagious. He doesn't just think the game; he gives the team its attitude.""He's got that dog in him" (Photo: Kamil Krzaczynski, USA TODAY Sports) That mentality shows up in the fire Cadeau brings to every game. Boynton said the team often feeds off his energy and edge. "He's got that 'dog' in him, and we need that," Boynton said. "Being a 6-1 point guard, he has no choice but to be relentless every minute. He sets the tone for us." Cadeau's defense and mindset have also helped Michigan reach a new level this season. "One of the underrated aspects of Elliot's game is his defensive ability," Boynton noted. "As a staff, we said, 'how do we get to the next level? One of the things we have to do is get Elliot and Yax to turn up their level defensively.' That coincided with us going to Vegas and molly-whopping three really good teams. We came back and were like, holy cow, we can challenge these guys also. We were like, man, this thing has a chance to be really, really special." Boynton said Cadeau's ability to think the game multiple steps ahead. It has made him the team's brain on the floor. "You see him make a pass or a cut and you just go, 'What was that?'… in a good way," Boynton said. "He's seeing things before anyone else sees them. His instincts, timing, and chemistry with his teammates are uncommon."March Roddy (Photo: Kamil Krzaczynski, USA TODAY Sports) It's also uncommon to see a player recover from the kind of struggles Roddy Gayle Jr. faced. That's why seeing both of them step up has been so special. "Roddy Gayle, first of all, he took a lot of flak for coming here from the other school. He stood in the fire, man," Boynton said. "Even in times where he struggled, he hasn't backed down from the noise… Yesterday's game turned because it was kind of a tight game there for the first couple of minutes. His tip-dunk loosened the game up for us. Then we started getting stops and rebounds, and he hit the transition three, and that really broke the dam. I couldn't be more proud of anybody." Boynton said Gayle became a key player in the postseason, earning the nickname "March Roddy" last year, thanks to his perseverance and humility. He added that Gayle has been even better this year. "I'll be honest. I think it all plays a part. I don't think you have March Roddy without January Roddy," Boynton said. "In January, I told him, man, you will be nice. He couldn't make a shot. Roddy forgot how to play basketball. He couldn't dribble. He couldn't catch a ball. He couldn't stand on his feet. He was falling all over the place. He forgot what size and what shape the ball was a few times. I was like, " What am I watching? In a bad way."“It’s great to see good guys win” (Photo: Kamil Krzaczynski, USA TODAY Sports) Through all the adversity, Gayle never wavered. "When you go through those struggles, your character is really revealed," Boynton said. "What he did, which was impressive to me in those moments… he showed up every day with a good attitude. He never pointed the finger at his teammates or his coaches. He never said, 'I made a mistake coming here; I regret my decision.' It was. I'm going to figure this out. Obviously, he was right." That resilience has paid off and made Gayle one of Michigan's most important players on both offense and defense. "He works his butt off. He cares about people," Boynton said. "He came back this year expecting his role to be bigger. For him to have what would be considered from the outside world a lesser role… playing less minutes, taking less shots, scoring less points… (but still impact winning with) his defensive ability and the spark he brings to us offensively… I couldn't be more proud of anybody than I am of him and what he's done." Boynton added, "It's great to see good guys win. He's a good dude. He works his tail off, and he's handled every bit of adversity with maturity. Now, he's reaping every bit of what he's sown."“A heavy-weight battle” (Photo: USA TODAY Sports) Now, Michigan's unselfish and determined team is just one win away from the national championship game. Their next challenge is the Arizona Wildcats, coached by Tommy Lloyd and known for their depth and physical style. "When you watch Arizona, [they're a] complete team," Boynton said. "You see, first and foremost, they play big-boy basketball. There's a bunch of grown men out there playing against their little brothers most nights and making it look easy." "It's going to be a heck of a matchup because both teams have incredible size across the board," Boynton added. "Both strengths are the physicality that each team plays with. You're looking at a heavy-weight battle. Two great coaches. I know Tommy very, very well from my USA Basketball experience. His ability to adapt from year to year, depending on his roster, has been impressive." Boynton highlighted the Wildcats' depth despite the roster turnover from last season. "People forget that they lost a lottery pick last year. The kid who plays for the Spurs, Carter Bryant, was on that team as a freshman last year," he said. "North Carolina's starting center, who I think was an All-ACC player, was on Arizona last year. Caleb Love was in Arizona last year. He plays in the NBA for the Blazers. [Lloyd's] ability to adapt to a new roster with essentially a lot of freshmen, which most people aren't doing, has been impressive."Arizona standing in the way (Photo: USA TODAY Sports) The individual matchups, Boynton said, are "must-watch" basketball. "You talk about Jaden Bradley versus Elliot Cadeau. You talk about Yax and Koa Peat… that'll be a storyline," Boynton said. "You talk about Tobe Awaka's force with Morez Johnson Jr.. You have two seven-plus-foot centers from Europe in Krivas and Aday. You have a really, really balanced matchup that's going to take a heck of a game plan and even better execution for a team to win on Saturday night." Boynton summed up the stakes succinctly: "When two teams this talented, this complete, and this connected meet, there's not going to be much separating them. It's about toughness, execution, and who can stay true to what's gotten them there." Michigan's journey from preseason potential to Final Four particpant has been a story of vision, character, and collective sacrifice. And with the nation watching, the Wolverines have no intention of stopping now. As Boynton put it simply: "We're one win away from being able to play for the ultimate goal in this game… to play on the final Monday."‘The job’s not done’ as Michigan heads to the Final Four, prepares for ‘heavyweight’ battle with ArizonaMichigan men's basketball is en route to the Final Four, departing Ann Arbor on Wednesday afternoon before a throng of supporters who crowded the William Davidson Player…Michigan men's basketball is en route to the Final Four, departing Ann Arbor on Wednesday afternoon before a throng of supporters who crowded the William Davidson Player Development Center to wish them well. For Dusty May and part of his staff, this weekend represents their second visit to the Final Four. In 2023, his Florida Atlantic team reached college basketball's last weekend. It was a special experience, May remembered this week in a conversation with Brian Boesch and Jordan Morgan, but his Wolverines are approaching the weekend differently than the Owls did three years ago. "Last time it was like, 'Wow! We're in the Final Four.' And with this group, it's more like, 'Okay, we've got work to do,'" May said. "We still have two more games to accomplish our goals. And so even [Sunday] night for us not celebrating and having a water fight showed the mindset of our group that the job's not done."May called his first Final Four experience "mesmerizing," remembering the first time he walked into NRG Stadium and saw the basketball court surrounded by the stands of a football stadium. It's a whirlwind week, he recalled, with outside attention that makes for easy distractions. "Once we get to Indianapolis, we're going to go and lock down at certain periods," May said. "We're going to let them enjoy their family and share the experience at times, but as we get closer to the games, we're going to lock it down and try to stay in our normal routine." Elliot Cadeau suffers allergic reaction, will travel separately Michigan point guard Elliot Cadeau suffered an allergic reaction on Wednesday and will travel to Indianapolis later Wednesday, the program confirmed in a statement. "Before the team departed the Player Development Center today, Elliot alerted the medical staff that he may have had an allergic reaction to something that he ate. The doctors evaluated Elliot and he is fine. Out of an abundance of caution, he is receiving medical supervision and will be traveling to Indianapolis later today." The Wolverines will start practicing at Lucas Oil Stadium on Thursday. Dusty May previews matchup with Arizona Michigan and Arizona have remained near the top of the national rankings throughout the 2025-26 season, and their Final Four matchup represents a battle between two of the top-five teams in the KenPom era. Dusty May said he's watched the Wildcats throughout the season and sees similarities with the Wolverines. "They're fun to watch. They're a lot like us where they have some older guys that made a lot of sacrifices to win and to be in the position they're in," May said. "They're incredibly physical. They run the floor. They pound the paint off the bounce, off the post, especially on the offensive glass. We got a little segue with Tennessee as far as their physicality, but it's going to be two heavyweights going at it. This isn't a featherweight fight. This is two heavyweights going at it. It's going to be fun to compete against those guys because we have a lot of respect for the history of the program, their current players, and their coaching." Arizona has a top-five offense and defense, per KenPom. They take among the fewest 3-pointers in the country but are excellent inside the arc and on the glass. "They put pressure on the rim and they attack," May said. "And so whenever they can create a good shot, then they take it. They won't take the quick 3s that we take, which obviously improves our tempo. But they're a team that lives and thrives inside the 3-point line. And so I hopefully will be able to use our 3-point shooting as an advantage to this game. But it's also one of the reasons why they're so good on the offensive glass."A lot of their misses are soft around the rim and they're so big and physical, they're rooting you under the rim and blocking you in. So they're going to present a number of challenges. It gives me anxiety thinking about all their weapons and Koa Peat and the size that they have. They're a special group."The Wolverines and Wildcats tip off at 8:49 p.m. ET on Saturday, April 4. Story photo by Marc-Gregor Campredon / MGoBlog.com.
